units.title: Python 3 began as a fix for Python 2
units.summary: Python 2.0 shipped in 2000. PEP 3000 (2006) planned Python 3 as a deliberate break in compatibility; Python 3.0 shipped in December 2008.

claims.text: PEP 3000, created in 2006, planned Python 3 to break backwards compatibility.

refs.quote: Python 3.0 will break backwards compatibility with Python 2.x.

units.title: Eleven years of two Pythons
units.summary: Python 2.7 (2010) was the last 2.x release; its end of life was moved in 2014 to 2020 for users who could not yet migrate.

claims.text: Python 2.7 is the end of the 2.x series.

refs.quote: Python 2.7 is the end of the Python 2.x series, and is succeeded by Python 3.

claims.text: End of life was moved five years, to 2020, in April 2014.

refs.quote: The End Of Life date (EOL, sunset date) for Python 2.7 has been moved five years into the future, to 2020.
Python 2.7 is the end of the Python 2.x series, and is succeeded by Python 3.

units.title: 1 January 2020: Python 2 support stops
units.summary: Support for Python 2.7 officially stopped on 1 January 2020.

units.title: After the split: yearly releases, speed, no GIL
units.summary: Since 3.9 a feature release ships every October; 3.11 was 10–60% faster than 3.10; 3.13 added an experimental mode without the GIL.

claims.text: Feature releases ship every twelve months, starting with 3.9.

refs.quote: feature versions are released predictably every twelve months, in October every year
This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python starting with Python 3.9.
Python 3.11 is between 10-60% faster than Python 3.10.

claims.text: 3.13 can run with the GIL disabled, experimentally.

refs.quote: CPython now has experimental support for running in a free-threaded mode, with the global interpreter lock (GIL) disabled.

claims.text: Ending Python 2 freed effort for this work.
